issues.description: The reported final sample size is inconsistent across Methods and Results/Tables. Methods states a final sample of N = 372 after exclusions, but Table 1 and Table 2 report N = 321, and Table 3 reports N = 244. The manuscript does not reconcile these discrepancies or explain additional case loss between the stated final sample and the analytic samples. This undermines transparency and makes it difficult to evaluate power, attrition, and generalizability of the analyses.
issues.quote:
This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.
...
Note. N = 321.
...
Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: The exclusion counts are arithmetically inconsistent with the reported final sample. Starting from 468 at T1, excluding 16 for missing time points and 78 for poor data quality would yield 374, not 372. The manuscript also states 56 failed demographic consistency and 1 exceeded 50% missingness, totaling 57, not 78. This suggests either undocumented exclusion criteria or errors in reporting, which raises concerns about data handling integrity.
issues.quote:
n = 468 nurses responded at time 1
...
Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample.
...
This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.
...
(a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 ...); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1).

issues.description: Participants who missed any wave were not invited to subsequent waves. This design converts intermittent missingness into permanent dropout by protocol, likely inducing nonrandom attrition and reducing representativeness of later waves. It also prevents use of standard longitudinal missing-data approaches that assume participants could continue after occasional missed waves. The weak comparison provided does not adequately rule out attrition bias.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys).

issues.description: The analytic sample was restricted to participants who completed all four surveys. Complete-case analysis in longitudinal data can bias estimates unless data are missing completely at random, which is not established here. Given the design-induced dropout and additional moderator missingness, the decision to analyze only completers threatens validity and likely wastes available information.
issues.quote: Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) ... were included in the final sample.

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges missingness on perceived patient acuity, including invalid responses, but does not specify how these missing values were handled analytically beyond using a reduced sample in Table 3. There is no justification for complete-case analysis, no imputation/model-based treatment, no missingness diagnostics, and no assessment of whether missingness was systematic. Because the moderation analyses lose a large share of cases, this may bias interaction estimates and substantially reduce power.
issues.quote:
Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).
...
Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: The paper states that patient acuity had missing data but does not report how many values were missing overall, at which wave(s), or what proportion of the sample was affected. This omission prevents readers from evaluating the seriousness of the missing-data problem and the credibility of the moderation analyses.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank ... or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range ...

issues.description: All core variables—including predictor, mediators, moderator, and outcome—were measured by the same respondents using self-report surveys. Temporal separation helps but does not eliminate shared method bias, especially for morally charged self-reports like enacted incivility. Common rater effects, consistency motifs, and negative affectivity could inflate associations among repeated measures.
issues.quote:
Data were collected at four time points across four consecutive weeks...
...
This study is a four-wave panel longitudinal design that will include administration of self-report online questionnaires...
...
First, our data were collected using self-report questionnaires.

issues.description: Enacted incivility toward patients is a socially undesirable behavior with possible professional consequences. Sole reliance on self-report is especially problematic here, as respondents may underreport harmful patient-directed behavior. The manuscript does not discuss social desirability controls, assurances beyond confidentiality, or validation against alternative sources.
issues.quote: Enacted Incivility. Four items from the Enacted Incivility Scale ... were used to measure the frequency participants instigated incivility towards their patients.

issues.description: Patient acuity is conceptualized as severity and intensity of nursing care required, yet it is measured with a single self-estimated percentage of patients considered 'severe.' This departs from the construct definition by reducing a multidimensional workload construct to a rough subjective proportion. It also conflates acuity with caseload composition, and may not capture intensity, workload, or care complexity in a comparable way across departments.
issues.quote: Patient acuity is defined as “a measure of the severity of illness of the patient and the intensity of nursing care that patient requires” ... we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.description: The acuity item asks respondents to rely on their department's scale and gives examples spanning very different specialties and types of assessment, including instruments not clearly intended as general nurse workload/acuity metrics. This likely introduces substantial measurement non-equivalence across respondents because 'severe' is anchored to different tools and contexts in different units.
issues.quote: Based on your department's patient acuity scale ... Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools”.

issues.description: Perceived patient acuity is measured by a single ad hoc item. While pilots assessed comprehension, the manuscript provides no evidence of reliability, temporal stability, convergent/discriminant validity, or relation to objective acuity. Using an unvalidated single-item moderator is especially concerning because interaction effects are sensitive to measurement error.
issues.quote: Within this study, we look at perceptions of patient acuity across all patients seen within a given work week ... by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.description: Some enacted incivility items may not map well onto nurse–patient interactions, particularly items about doubting patients' judgment 'on a matter over which they had responsibility.' In clinical settings, disagreement about patient judgment can reflect legitimate care or safety decisions rather than incivility. This risks construct contamination by professional role behavior.
issues.quote: “Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility”

issues.description: The manuscript frames the study as patient incivility, emotions toward patients, and enacted incivility toward patients, but the measures combine patients with family members/friends. This broad aggregation obscures whether effects are driven by patients, families, or both, and may distort interpretation because family interactions differ structurally from patient interactions.
issues.quote:
the customers are the patients and their families.
...
participants were asked ... any of your patients or patient family members/friends…
...
Thinking about your interactions with patients during the past week, how often have you…?

issues.description: Variables are labeled inconsistently as customer incivility versus patient incivility across tables and text. Although the authors note adapting customer to patient wording, this inconsistent nomenclature creates ambiguity about whether the same construct is being analyzed throughout and complicates interpretation of tables.
issues.quote:
Patient Incivility. Patient incivility was assessed...
...
Table 1 ... T1 Customer Incivility ... T2 Customer Incivility
...
Hypothesis 1 predicted a positive relationship between experienced patient incivility and negative emotions towards patients.

issues.description: The CFA fit report omits the chi-square symbol/degrees-of-freedom formatting, making the test statistic uninterpretable. As written, '(269) = 862.05' is incomplete. Precise reporting is necessary for readers to assess model fit and compare to alternatives.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99)

issues.description: The discriminant validity section is incomplete. The manuscript says the four-factor model fit better than alternative models with fewer factors, but it does not report the alternative models, their fit indices, chi-square differences, factor correlations, or whether the CFA used one wave or pooled data. This limits evaluation of discriminant validity, particularly given the very high intercorrelations among constructs.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable ... and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.

issues.description: For Hypothesis 4, the manuscript states that the serial indirect effect to enacted incivility was estimated by multiplying 'the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).' In a serial mediation from X to M1 to M2 to Y, the indirect effect should involve all constituent paths (e.g., a × d × b), not just two paths. This is a substantive statistical error in describing the model and raises concern that the indirect effect may have been miscomputed or at minimum misreported.
issues.quote: Finally, Hypothesis 4 predicted that experienced patient incivility would be positively indirectly related to enacted incivility toward patients through negative emotions toward patients and compassion fatigue. Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).

issues.description: The coefficient for the direct path from T2 customer incivility to T4 enacted incivility differs between the text and Table 2. The results text and Table 2 are not aligned on this crucial path, which raises concern about transcription accuracy and model specification consistency.
issues.quote:
Table 2 ... T2 Customer Incivility ... Enacted Incivility (T4) B = -.07, SE = .05, t = -1.14
...
First, using the native lm() function in R ... experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40)

issues.description: The coefficient for negative emotions predicting enacted incivility differs notably between Table 2 and the supplemental regression. Table 2 reports B = .28, whereas the supplemental OLS regression reports B = .23. Different analytic models may yield different estimates, but the manuscript does not clearly explain the difference in specifications or why these should be compared to claim one predictor is 'six times' stronger. This creates interpretive confusion.
issues.quote:
Table 2 ... T3 Negative Emotions ... Enacted Incivility (T4) .28**
...
First, using the native lm() function in R ... negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.description: The supplemental analysis claims the compassion fatigue parameter estimate is nearly six times that of negative emotions, but Table 2 shows .57 versus .28, which is roughly two times, not six. Moreover, unstandardized coefficients from different predictors are not directly comparable as evidence of stronger effects unless scales are commensurate and model conditions justify it. The rationale for the relative importance analysis is therefore based on a mathematically incorrect premise.
issues.quote:
the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions.
...
Table 2 ... T3 Negative Emotions ... Enacted Incivility (T4) .28** ...
T4 Compassion Fatigue ... Enacted Incivility (T4) .57***

issues.description: The manuscript states that predictors 'accounted for' 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility. Relative importance weights partition the model's explained variance among predictors, not total outcome variance. The language used overstates what the analysis shows and may mislead readers into treating these as absolute variance explained. In addition, one predictor was nonsignificant, so interpreting it as accounting for nearly a quarter of variance requires caution.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.description: The reported correlations and R² values are extremely high for conceptually related but distinct self-report constructs measured across weeks (e.g., .96 correlation between T3 negative emotions and T4 compassion fatigue; R² = .81 for enacted incivility). Such magnitudes raise concerns about multicollinearity, construct redundancy, common method inflation, or coding/reporting errors, yet the manuscript does not address these issues. These values directly challenge discriminant validity and the stability of regression estimates.
issues.quote:
T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .96
...
R2 ... Enacted Incivility ... .81

issues.description: The near-unity correlation between negative emotions and compassion fatigue across adjacent waves suggests these constructs may not be empirically distinct in this dataset, despite being treated as separate serial mediators. This threatens the validity of the serial mediation interpretation because the model may be partitioning the same underlying distress construct into two mediators.
issues.quote: Table 1 ... T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue | .96

issues.description: The manuscript references 'controls' and tables note 'with Time 1 Controls,' but the rationale for selecting work hours, whether baseline levels of focal constructs were controlled, and whether the same covariate set was preregistered or consistently applied is not explained. Longitudinal mediation claims are sensitive to control strategy, especially autoregressive controls. The omission leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote:
This allowed us to assess the covariances between all variables (including controls) within each wave...
...
Table 1 | Correlation and Descriptive Information for Hypothesized Model with Time 1 Controls
...
Table 2 includes T2 Work Hours and T3 Work Hours only.

issues.description: The models appear not to control for prior levels of the mediator and outcome variables (e.g., T2 negative emotions when predicting T3 negative emotions, T3 enacted incivility when predicting T4 enacted incivility, or baseline compassion fatigue). Without autoregressive controls, the analyses do not estimate change over time and are vulnerable to stable individual differences driving associations. This substantially weakens longitudinal inference.
issues.quote:
We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2).
...
In the second step (path d), Time 3 negative emotions toward patients were positively related to Time 4 compassion fatigue...
...
Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients...

issues.description: The paper repeatedly uses causal language ('leads to', 'impacts', 'drive', 'through which this is occurring') despite relying on observational self-report panel data without randomization, strong confound control, or autoregressive modeling. Temporal ordering alone does not justify these causal conclusions, and the manuscript overstates the capacity for causal inference.
issues.quote:
These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.
...
allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time.

issues.description: Potential confounds such as trait negative affectivity, hostility, burnout proneness, unit climate, staffing ratios, shift type, and organizational incivility climate could plausibly influence both experienced and enacted incivility, as well as negative emotions and fatigue. The manuscript does not measure or control for these factors, limiting interpretability of purported process effects.
issues.quote:
To better understand the effect of the predictor variables on the criterion variable at the subsequent time point...
...
Table 2 includes T2 Work Hours and T3 Work Hours only.

issues.description: The manuscript introduces social learning theory but then describes the stressor-emotion model of counterproductive work behavior. These are distinct frameworks, yet the text conflates them by calling 'this model' social learning theory and then summarizing Spector & Fox's stressor-emotion model. This conceptual confusion weakens theoretical coherence.
issues.quote: To understand how incivility experiences from customers may be impacting employee affect and behavior over time, we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977). This model considers how individuals learn behaviors through observation and modeling of others' actions and their consequences, ultimately shaping counterproductive work behaviors (CWB), such as enacted incivility. Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005).

issues.description: The compassion fatigue section states the study examines experiencing coworker incivility, whereas the study otherwise focuses on patient/customer incivility. This appears to be a conceptual and editorial inconsistency that could confuse readers about the actual source being modeled.
issues.quote: Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue.

issues.description: The narrative for Hypothesis 4 describes a serial indirect effect through negative emotions and compassion fatigue, yet labels it a 'simple mediation' in discussing the 'last step,' and mis-specifies the indirect product. This inconsistency between conceptual model and statistical description makes it unclear exactly what model was estimated.
issues.quote:
Hypothesis 4 predicted ... through negative emotions toward patients and compassion fatigue.
...
the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue...

issues.description: Recruitment relied heavily on flyers, social networks, professional contacts, and online groups, with self-initiated participation and no clear verification procedures beyond self-report screening. This raises concerns about ineligible participation, duplicate responding, and uncontrolled sampling bias, especially because no institutional sampling frame or employment verification is described.
issues.quote:
Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies...
...
For all recruitment strategies, participants initiated the contact and study procedures by clicking on the study link or QR code...
...
To help ensure that the participants were from healthcare contexts, we highlighted the nursing focus in the recruitment and consent information and directly asked participants if they met the inclusion criteria.

issues.description: The discussion extends findings to 'service industries' and customer incivility generally, despite a nonprobability sample of nurses in high-stakes care settings, mostly women, with potentially unique ethical and power dynamics. Such extrapolation is not justified without replication in other service occupations and contexts.
issues.quote:
Because incivility from customers is likely a common experience for employees in the service industries...
...
The purpose of this four-wave study was to examine the trickle-down effects of experiencing customer incivility (a common occurrence within the service industries)...

issues.description: The sample is overwhelmingly female and limited to high-stakes nursing settings. Although this reflects the profession to some extent, the manuscript underplays how gender composition, profession-specific norms, and hospital hierarchies may shape both incivility exposure and enactment. These limitations constrain external validity.
issues.quote:
The majority of respondents were female (96.64%)...
...
All participants were currently employed as a nurse ... and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.description: The paper does not report how many hospitals ultimately contributed participants, whether participants were nested within hospitals/units, geographic distribution, or unit types represented. These omissions hinder evaluation of clustering, contextual confounds, and sample heterogeneity.
issues.quote:
Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S....
...
three hospitals local to the research team...
...
our sample includes nurses within high-stakes patient care settings.

issues.description: Participants were recruited from hospitals and likely units/departments, but analyses treat observations as independent. If nurses are clustered within hospitals or units, standard errors may be underestimated and contextual influences ignored. The manuscript provides no intraclass correlations, cluster counts, or multilevel adjustments.
issues.quote:
Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S....
...
At each location, we asked the manager/head of the department to post the fliers in employee common areas...

issues.description: The manuscript does not provide enough detail to reproduce the analyses: centering of interaction terms, estimator used for structural models, whether variables were latent or observed in the mediation models, how confidence intervals were generated in Mplus, and full syntax/model equations are absent. This impedes replication and appraisal of analytic choices.
issues.quote:
we followed procedures described by Edwards and Lambert (2007), Hayes (2015, 2017), Preacher et al. (2007), and Selig and Preacher (2009) to estimate direct and indirect effects...
...
We then used a Monte Carlo simulation with 20,000 replications ...

issues.description: There is no mention of preregistration, a registered analysis plan, or distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses. Given multiple waves, several possible lag structures, shortened scales, moderator analyses, and supplemental tests, undisclosed analytic flexibility is a concern.
issues.quote: Supplemental analyses. We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility.

issues.description: The study selected only the 'highest loading items' from scales to shorten surveys. While pragmatic, selecting items based on loadings can narrow construct breadth and capitalize on sample-specific properties. The evidence offered is limited and does not fully establish that the shortened versions preserve content validity in this context, especially for enacted incivility.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability (Maloney et al., 2011).

issues.description: The quantitative pilot used MTurk workers who reportedly were nurses in high-stakes settings. For a specialized licensed population, MTurk recruitment raises concerns about credential verification and relevance of pilot validity evidence. The manuscript does not explain how these pilot participants were authenticated as nurses.
issues.quote: The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses who worked in high-stakes settings and were recruited from MTurk.

issues.description: For the novel acuity item and shortened scales, the pilot evidence primarily concerns understandability and applicability rather than substantive validity, reliability, or criterion alignment. This is insufficient support for central measures, especially a key moderator with substantial missingness and cross-context heterogeneity.
issues.quote:
The quantitative pilot survey included all final survey items ... and additional questions asking about relevance and clarity of items.
...
all participants provided an answer ... responded that they felt capable of accurately responding to the item, and that it was applicable to their patients.

issues.description: The tables contain several formatting/reporting irregularities that obscure interpretation, including repeated headers, malformed arrows in indirect paths, an R² value shown as '.', duplicated B columns in Table 3, and missing significance markers consistency. These issues suggest insufficient statistical reporting quality control.

When the sample drops from 321 to 244 for moderation analyses, the manuscript does not provide descriptive comparisons between included and excluded cases on key variables. Without this, readers cannot assess whether the moderation sample is selectively biased.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: Given the literature cited on reciprocal effects and the high temporal stability likely present, alternative directional paths are plausible: nurses who enact incivility or have compassion fatigue may perceive more incivility from patients or report more negative emotions later. The paper does not model reciprocal or cross-lagged alternatives, so claims of a unidirectional process are premature.
issues.quote:
Previous studies have shown that lags spanning this length of time are sufficient ...
...
allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time.

issues.description: The one-week lag is justified by citing studies on counterproductive behavior generally, but no construct-specific rationale is given for why negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility should unfold sequentially over exactly weekly intervals. If the lag is misspecified, mediation pathways may be distorted or missed.
issues.quote: Previous studies have shown that lags spanning this length of time are sufficient for observing emergence of such counterproductive behaviors as incivility and that the observed effects will not meaningfully differ from studies featuring longer periods of time between waves.

issues.description: The compassion fatigue measure includes items spanning hopelessness and losing sleep over patients' trauma. In this study it is used as a downstream consequence of patient incivility and as a mediator to enacted incivility, but many items may reflect general occupational distress or trauma exposure unrelated to incivility. This makes the proposed mechanism less specific than interpreted.
issues.quote: Example items include “I have felt a sense of hopelessness associated with working with patients” and “I am losing sleep over a patient’s traumatic experiences.”

issues.description: Compassion fatigue is defined as arising from prolonged exposure to others' suffering and trauma, including secondary trauma. Using patient incivility as a primary antecedent may be theoretically plausible but is not well integrated with this definition. The manuscript leans on overlap with burnout to justify the measure, which risks concept stretching and weakens precision of the proposed mechanism.
issues.quote:
Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components...
...
Secondary trauma can be thought of as the vicarious experience of another person’s trauma...
...
Due to the persistent relationships between job demands, such as incivility, fatigue, and strain experiences ... and the conceptual overlap between burnout and compassion fatigue, we believe this relationship will replicate with a caregiving-specific form of burnout

issues.description: Although alphas appear in Table 1 for some T1/T2/T3/T4 measures, the manuscript does not systematically report reliability estimates for each scale at each wave in the text, especially for the shortened scales and the final analytic sample(s). For a repeated-measures design using adapted instruments, fuller reliability reporting is warranted.
issues.quote: Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal.

issues.description: The wave counts imply 450 respondents at T4, yet only 16 were excluded for missing time points relative to the T1 sample of 468, which would leave 452 complete cases before quality exclusions. This does not align with the stated final N = 372 or table Ns, indicating unresolved inconsistencies in participant flow.
issues.quote:
n = 468 nurses responded at time 1; ... n = 450 responded at time 4 ...
...
Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) ...
...
This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.
